prompt:
Machine learning needs data management too:
a) What are the main challenges and tasks of data management for machine learning?
b) Why does preparation dominate the effort?
hints: Follow the data from several raw sources to a trained model.
What happens to the model when the training data is dirty?
Which of the course's other topics reappear here at larger scale?
keyPoints: Collection and integration: training data comes from several sources and must be combined and conformed
Cleaning: errors, duplicates, missing values, inconsistencies - a model trained on dirty data learns the dirt ('garbage in, garbage out')
Transformation: feature construction, normalization, encoding; reduction and sampling for tractability
Scale: training sets can be very large, so storage and preprocessing must be scalable
Governance: privacy restricts what data may be used; reproducibility needs dataset versioning and provenance
Preparation dominates the KDD effort: the mining step itself is often the small, well-tooled part
modelAnswer: Machine learning lives or dies by its data, and managing that data is a set of real tasks. First, collection and integration: training data usually comes from several sources and must be found, combined and conformed. Second, cleaning: real data has errors, duplicates, missing values and inconsistencies, and a model trained on dirty data learns the dirt - garbage in, garbage out. Third, transformation: features must be constructed, normalized and encoded, and the data reduced or sampled so training is tractable. Fourth, scale: training sets can be very large, so storage and preprocessing must be scalable - which connects to the warehouse and distributed-systems parts of the course. Fifth, governance: privacy law restricts what data may be used, and reproducibility requires versioning, so you know exactly which data produced which model. Preparation dominates the effort because every step before the mining is data management: the mining algorithms themselves are usually the small, well-tooled part of the pipeline.
followUps: Which of these tasks would you automate, and which need human judgement?
How does a data warehouse support exactly these preparation steps?

prompt: Explain the stages of the KDD (Knowledge Discovery in Databases) process.
hints: The process starts long before any mining algorithm runs.
Name the stages in order, from raw data to something someone can act on.
Which stages dominate the effort in practice?
keyPoints: Selection: determine the application domain and choose the relevant data
Preprocessing: clean the data - noise, missing values, duplicates
Transformation: reduce, aggregate, select or construct the features the mining methods will see
Data mining: apply the methods (classification, clustering, regression, association rules) to find patterns
Interpretation/evaluation: validate, visualize and turn patterns into usable knowledge
The process is iterative, and the stages before mining dominate the total effort
modelAnswer: The KDD process describes how to get from raw data to useful knowledge in stages. First, selection: determine the application domain and choose which data is relevant for the goal. Second, preprocessing: clean the selected data - remove noise, handle missing values and duplicates, and make the data usable at all. Third, transformation: reduce the data where it is too large, aggregate it, and select or construct the features that the mining methods will actually see. Fourth, data mining: this is the step that gives the process its name - applying methods such as classification, clustering, regression or association rules to find patterns. Fifth, interpretation and evaluation: the patterns must be checked for validity and usefulness, visualized, and turned into knowledge someone can act on. The process is iterative - a bad result sends you back to selection or preprocessing - and in practice the first three stages dominate the effort, while the mining step itself is often the smallest and best supported by tools.
followUps: Give an example of a 'pattern' that is valid but not useful.
Where in the KDD process would a data warehouse sit?

prompt: Describe the life cycle of a data warehouse.
hints: Start from what the business needs, not from the source databases.
A warehouse needs a constant pipeline from the operational systems.
Ask what happens after the first reports run - the warehouse is never 'done'.
keyPoints: Requirements: the analyses and business decisions the warehouse must support, per process (sales, logistics, ...)
Design: a dimensional model - fact tables with measures surrounded by dimensions - instead of a normalized ER schema
Build ETL: extract from operational sources, transform (clean and conform), load into the warehouse
Use: reporting and OLAP analysis, often through data marts targeted at specific user groups
Maintain and evolve: refresh cycles, quality monitoring, tuning, adding new facts, dimensions and sources
The cycle is long and iterative - the warehouse grows with the organization
modelAnswer: A data warehouse is built in a life cycle of its own, roughly: requirements, design, build, populate, use, and maintain. It starts from the business side: the analyses and decisions the warehouse must support, usually thought of per business process, like sales or logistics. From that comes the design: a dimensional model - fact tables holding measures, surrounded by dimensions like time, product and store - rather than a normalized ER schema, because the workload is analysis, not transactions. Then the ETL machinery is built: extraction from the operational sources, transformation to clean and conform the data, and load into the warehouse. Once populated, it serves reporting and OLAP analysis, often through data marts targeted at particular user groups. And finally the maintenance loop: regular refreshes from the sources, monitoring of quality and load times, tuning, and evolution - new facts, dimensions and sources are added as the organization's needs change, so a warehouse is never really finished.
followUps: Why is the dimensional model preferred over a normalized ER model inside the warehouse?
What happens to the warehouse when an operational source changes its schema?

prompt:
Relational data warehouse design schemas:
a) Explain the star, snowflake and fact constellation schemas.
b) What motivates each, and what are their disadvantages?
hints: All three put facts and dimensions in separate tables - the difference is what happens to the dimensions.
Ask how many joins a typical analysis query needs in each schema.
One of them models several business processes at once.
keyPoints: Star: one fact table with flat, denormalized dimension tables - simple and fast; disadvantage: redundancy in dimensions, awkward dimension updates
Snowflake: dimensions normalized into sub-dimensions - less redundancy, easier maintenance; disadvantage: more joins, slower and more complex queries
Fact constellation (galaxy): several fact tables sharing dimensions - models several business processes; disadvantage: large, complex schema, harder to design and query
All three separate facts (numerical measures) from dimensions (context) and suit the read-mostly OLAP workload
modelAnswer: All three are relational schemas for a warehouse; they differ in how the dimensions are shaped. A star schema has one large fact table holding measures and foreign keys, with one flat, denormalized dimension table per dimension around it. It is motivated by simplicity and speed: an analysis query joins facts to a few dimension tables and nothing more. Its disadvantage is redundancy in the dimensions - for example the same city repeated in many customer rows - which costs storage and makes updates of dimension data awkward. A snowflake schema normalizes the dimensions into sub-dimensions, splitting city and country out of customer, say. That removes redundancy and makes dimension data easier to maintain, but queries need more joins, so they become more complex and slower - bad exactly where the warehouse is used. A fact constellation, or galaxy schema, has several fact tables - one per business process, like sales and shipments - sharing dimension tables. It can model a whole organization in one warehouse, at the price of a bigger, more complex schema that is harder to design and query.
followUps: Which schema would you choose for a small warehouse with one fact source and why?
Why is redundancy less of a problem in a warehouse than in an operational database?
